utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down and good morning to you. Mr. Wubben, appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, and also good morning to the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I am here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones, I represent Mr. Naser Oric. Together with us, our legal assistant, Miss Adisa Mehic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Very short, Your Honours. It's good to be proactive, and with a view to Rule 98 bis we face a kind of new procedure, and Your Honours already touched base on that issue in the beginning of the trial. For the Prosecution, there are some questions regarding the timing, the procedure as such. It's not the content, but how it will follow up itself, meaning: Does the Prosecution have some time to prepare after submission, when a submission is done, of course, by Defence, or not, given in days or in week, and how should we see this new procedure as it will be one of the first proceedings with a view to oral hearing. Is it possible for this Trial Chamber to give some guidance, some instructions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Would you like to say something at this stage, before, because he just -- Mr. Wubben just --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sprung this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's as if he was reading my mind throughout the entire week. And in actual fact, we and our staff have been working on this, and my idea was to have a meeting, Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser and myself, sometime early next week to see that there is uniformity in our approach to the matter. And then, since I believe, at least for the time being - and this is what I will be suggesting to Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser - I think that this, the whole thing, which procedure should apply in the first place, whether it's the new one or the old one, and if it's the new one, how are we going to apply it? And if it's the old one, how are we going to apply it, considering that there is a pronouncement by the Judges of discontent with the old system. So my idea was, in this meeting that I will be having with the other two judges, to propose a short debate here in which you will be invited to make submissions, and that would entail finding, say, between half an hour -- half an hour, roughly, for submissions, 15 minutes each, and then you will receive a direction from us as to what the procedure will be and what to expect. But this will be done, hopefully, by the end of next week, because it has been on my mind and I have been labouring on it together with the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There indeed must be something in the air, Your Honour, because we ourselves yesterday found ourselves also turning to this subject and wondering what the time periods would be and what the procedure would be. As far as the new procedure, there's Rule 6(D) concerning when amendments come into effect, but I think for our part we assumed it would be the new system with oral submissions, and again we weren't sure whether it would be Prosecution responding immediately after us, or some delay, but the one -- that's obviously to be considered, but one concern we had is just that, given that it will be our motion, that we would have a right to reply in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. But you are probably right in thinking that it will be the new procedure that will be applied. But at least that's my personal opinion for the time being. I stand to be, of course -- I'm open to conviction on that, and it's a subject that we have not yet discussed. I'm being very clear about it. So the position of the Trial Chamber is reserved completely on that. There will be, however, an opportunity for you to make submissions on this. So sometime next week, towards the end of the week, and it will -- I suppose we should try to find a bracket on Wednesday, because Thursday we stop again now, next week. I think we are not sitting from Thursday onwards because of the Queen's birthday. Are we sitting on Thursday? Oh, I see, we are sitting on Thursday. So we could leave it until Thursday, then. We could leave it 'til Thursday. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But don't -- I just wanted to put your minds at rest that no decision will be taken without giving you the opportunity to make submissions on this matter, because it is something which is important. I mean, I am used to a system, I can tell you, where this is done immediately the Prosecution rests its case. Not even a five-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's the system I'm familiar with as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not even a five minute break, I mean, so ... The decision is taken orally by the Magistrate or by the Judge there and then, on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it's something that would have matured in the minds of Prosecutor, Defence and Judge or Magistrate, all along in the course of -- we are all usually familiar with the exercise, what it entails and where the line of demarcation is as regards evaluation of evidence. So it's no big deal in my country, and I know it is no big deal in your country, and it is no big deal in many other common law jurisdictions, except in some states in the US where it is a big deal. So...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I was saying we're happy with an immediate motion, provided there is an immediate response not a delayed response, but that is all to be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, we will not adopt a system which is typically Maltese or British. There will be time for elaborating a little bit an ordered, reasoned-out line of submissions, but in all probability that will be oral and not in written form. And I don't want even to let you think for a moment that we're talking of time frames similar to the ones we used to have until recently, where written motions, Rule 98 bis motions were in place, or were adopted. I mean, I'm definitely not thinking along those lines, but we will come to that next week. The other problem that we have today: We have to finish, because of the exigencies of one of the Judges, we have to finish between 1 and 1.15. 1.15 at the latest, at the very latest. So what I suggest is that we will have one break, instead of -- we will just have one break, which would be the full break, and we will try to break, instead of half past ten, if it is okay with the interpreters and everyone, we will try to break at quarter to eleven, 15 minutes later. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And then we will restart at 11.15 and we will finish at 1.00, with a few minutes plus, if needed. All right? Thanks. My secretary and the secretary of my two colleagues, Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, felt very uncomfortable about having to come here first thing in the morning, having to deal with a revised list of documents which -- not in as much as it cut down on the ones that they had selected for us the day before, but in as much they had to dig up fresh documents in a matter of five minutes, because they usually come here just a couple of minutes before we start the -- a few minutes before we start the sitting. Please try to avoid that as much as you can. I know that you were obviously working on it late in the evening yesterday, and I appreciate that. On the other hand, do keep in mind that each time this is done, there are problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. The Prosecution will keep that in mind in the future with respect to the practicalities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will, Ms. Richardson. I mean, it wasn't meant to be a criticism. It was meant to be a recommendation for the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. Anything from your side? None? None? Yes, the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. You may sit down. Good morning, Mr. Becirovic. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome again. We are going to proceed with the examination-in-chief, hopefully finish with it today, then we are going to stop 'til Monday. We will continue on Monday, because there are other things happening that need to be attended to. Yes, Ms. Richardson. I just remind you that you are still testifying under oath in terms of the -- pursuant to the solemn declaration that you entered yesterday. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Richardson [Continued]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Becirovic. Yesterday when we ended, you were --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- you had been handed a document. I would like you to -- I would like the usher's assistance in giving you that document again. I just have a few more questions with respect to it. It is Prosecution's Exhibit 532. It is on Sanction. I would like you to take a look at this list and I would ask you to please indicate for us, with respect to the different individuals, where exactly they were located; whether they were located in the PTT building or the information centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take them -- first group. On the first page, Hasanovic and Begic, where were they located, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know that these two persons were located in the Territorial Defence Staff building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for the organisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow me. I believe that what I am going to say is really important. As far as I know, this organisation was in place after the militarisation, not before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But that you told us already yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That you told us yesterday. In fact, you expressed your surprise that they are shown to have joined in 1992, when, according to you, this happened after the demilitarisation. Second list: Ahmetovic and Mehmedovic. Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Lovac building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And from the third list, where you have ten persons, including yourself, first question: Were they all located in the same building, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were all located in the same building, but not from the very beginning. They were not members of the same unit, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was -- which was this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the post office building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The PTT, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I don't know if you want to follow up with any further questions on this last answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, was anyone located in the information centre, any of the persons listed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go back to one of the persons listed, and that is number 1, the second list, and that's Ahmetovic, and it is indicated under his duties that he operated the package communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Whoever is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whoever is trying to highlight the name of the person mentioned is highlighting the wrong person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is the second list, Ahmetovic Nedzad, that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, if you could tell us, could you describe for us what a package communication system is.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Package communication is a combination of a laptop or another type of computer, with a radio equipment, and it was used for transmission of information from one point to another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what type -- I will rephrase the question. Did there come a time that one such system was located in Srebrenica? And, if so, could you tell us when.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As early as March 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how the system was acquired? Where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzad Ahmetovic came from Tuzla and brought it with him. He brought the equipment, so seven or maybe ten days after his arrival he was able to install it and operate it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the system, could you tell us whether or not it is a coded system? In other words, do you send and receive messages in some type of system that permits or allows for code?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This system did provide for the coding and decoding of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Ahmetovic the only person who operated this system?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzad Ahmetovic brought the equipment and trained, after a month or two months, I can't be sure of the period, he trained Senahid Mehmedovic and Hajrudin Siricic [phoen], and after that they helped him in his work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the system located? Is it correct it was -- I will rephrase the question. Where was the system located?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the Lovac building. Although on several occasions Nedzad was forced to change locations, because it was not always possible for him to establish contact from the Lovac building. Those locations were mostly in the suburbs of Srebrenica and on some surrounding hills. For example, Bojna hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you tell us what period of time in 1993 the equipment was moved and to where?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened from time to time. He would go to a house on Bojna hill. From there, it was easier for him to establish communication with Tuzla. It didn't happen often. He performed most of his work in the Lovac building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this system work throughout 1993? Was it operational?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1994 as well?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, on two occasions the system broke down. The system software had problems and they could not work for seven days on two occasions. And that's at least what Nedzad told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself use the system during 1993 or in 1994?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not use the system. I wasn't trained to do it. And I couldn't use it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use it -- when I say "use it," and I guess I should qualify when I say "use," did you take messages to Ahmetovic or the other persons he trained to transmit the messages for you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, I think I sent a few messages using this system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1993, could you tell us whether or not - if you know - what places were contacted via this package communication system. In other words, was it Tuzla, Sarajevo, or any other part of the country?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know today, and as far as I knew then, it was mostly contacts with Tuzla that were established through this package system from its arrival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is with respect to persons who had access to the system. And by that, I mean persons who were able to give messages to the operator to communicate messages for them. Could you tell us whether or not any of the individuals in Srebrenica was able to use the system? Any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. officials, or anyone, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the demilitarisation and in 1994 and 1995, this system was used by the civilian authorities in Srebrenica and their organs, as well as by the military organs. I'm not aware whether this centre was under somebody's control and, if so, whose. I know that when they attempted to establish the municipal court in Srebrenica through the president of War Presidency, they used to send in certain questions and receive a response from Sarajevo. In addition to that, the president of the War Presidency used this system in order to inform the state organs in Bosnia-Herzegovina about the situation which existed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that the military organ authority would use it. Do you know who in the military would use the system?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that that existed until 1995, when the 28th Division was established. From that time on, I knew that the organs of the 28th Division in Srebrenica used the system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. With respect to the 28th Division, without giving them a name per se, did any members of the Territorial Defence, if that's what you knew it to be during 1992 and 1993, did any of those members use the system?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the PTT building --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm all done with this document. If the usher could take it from the witness, I would much appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the PTT building, could you tell us what organisations or which individuals used this building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The PTT building housed the service for communications and information headed by Hamed Alic. Members of this service are the people mentioned in the list. In addition to that, Nijaz Masic with another girl was there. I think that the girl's name was Elvedina Jamakovic. Their job was to collect statements of the deported residents from Bratunac municipality and nearby villages. They started doing this in June and July of 1992. These people had been expelled and suffered terrible tragedies. These two people collected statements from the deportees, and these statements, I assume, were to be used later as a testimony of the events taking place in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And anyone else? Did any other organisations?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As early as March, 1993, when the UNPROFOR commander for Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Morillon, arrived in Srebrenica, he housed his staff in the PTT building. Shortly thereafter, observers of the UN arrived. They also had their seat in the PTT building. And after the demilitarisation, the civilian police of the UN, if that's what it was called, was also housed in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the information centre, could you tell us which organisations, if any, or individuals, were located in the information centre.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre for information housed only the IC-745 equipment, which was used by the radio ham operators of the Srebrenica radio club, and their main task was to reestablish the broken lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "reestablish the broken lines," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he explained that yesterday. If you think he hasn't, you might as well go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly. If you did explain it yesterday, if you could just briefly recap exactly what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the first few months - meaning until August of 1992 - we mostly only collected information about certain individuals who had been deported from Bratunac to Tuzla. Perhaps as early as August or September and onwards, the radio station was also used for establishing contact with various persons. Civilians could come to the radio club in Srebrenica and sit by the radio ham operators whereas their family members who were in Tuzla or elsewhere could go to the local radio club where they could establish communication with their family members in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question specifically is, with respect to -- when you say -- so the broken lines is not cables. We're not talking about cables, we're talking about communication between relatives, so that we're clear?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many persons worked in the information centre?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially only Abid Zukic worked there. And later on, starting in September and October of 1992, there was another girl working with him. I can't remember her first and last name. Then after the demilitarisation, there was a group of young people there as well who had been trained in 1993 to use the radio equipment. And they worked there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to next move to the subject matter of Hamed Alic and specifically his duties. Did he supervise yourself and the other persons who worked in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Hamed supervised our work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also supervise the individuals who worked in the information centre?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wasn't tasked with supervising these people. That was not within his competencies, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what were his competencies?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understood it at that time, Hamed Alic was a man in charge of the post office in Bratunac. I think that he was put up there in that building because he had nowhere else to go, and also so that he could supervise how the telephone exchange and all the other equipment was used. At the time people expected that the war would be over soon and they thought that in order to protect the equipment -- they thought that it was important to protect the equipment so that it could be used later. After that, Hamed supervised the work of the people mentioned in the list. Sometime after, there was a power outage in the PTT building, I told you that we had a small generator and Hamed supervised the people operating the generator. In late 1993 it occurred to him that we could build the mini power plant that I mentioned yesterday, and once it was done, he also supervised the work of the power plant, or rather, the work of the people servicing the power plant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there, in addition to the ones you just mentioned, the operators and the girl who took information, did anyone else have any duties with respect to documenting the events of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. Yesterday my learned friend referred to duties on a couple of occasions and the witness never adopted the expression "duties." He would refer to "activities," and unless and until the witness is comfortable using the word "duties," I would prefer that my learned friend would refer to "activities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point taken, and I think he is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can ask the witness as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't really make much difference at the end of the day, but let's stick to the phraseology which was used yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, my question, I will rephrase it: Did anyone undertake activities or perform any action in Srebrenica regarding the documentation of the events that were occurring in and around Srebrenica, other than the recording -- other than the messages being sent?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've mentioned that these activities were conducted by Nijaz Masic [Realtime transcript read in error "Mustafic"] and the girl. In addition to the two of them, later on, in 1992, there were another two people there who had an amateur camera and recorded the footage of destruction in the town and nearby villages. They also recorded the looting that had taken place when the Serbs left the town earlier. For example, in the Jadar complex, all the machinery and all other equipment had been looted. So they recorded this footage with their amateur camera, intending to use it as evidence of the events that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment. I'm sorry to interrupt you, Ms. Richardson, but there is a little bit of confusion in the transcript here. It seems that part of what is attributed to you was said by Mr. Jones, the rest was said by myself and not by you. And we're talking of lines 15 to 17 of the previous page. After I said, "Point taken and I think he is right," the words, "It doesn't really make much difference at the end of the day but let's stick to the phraseology which was used yesterday, thank you," were used by me and not by you; and similarly, I think you didn't say the words, "We can ask the witness as well," so for the record, although these words are being attributed to you, they were -- they are not actually yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The individuals that you -- excuse me. The individuals that you mentioned who videotaped certain events in Srebrenica, did they work with Hamed Alic as well?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the type of work they conducted, yes, they did work with Hamed Alic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time I would like the usher's assistance in showing a document to the witness, and that will be Prosecution's Exhibit 79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a correction of the transcript. When the witness spoke about the persons who worked in the PTT building, he mentioned Nijaz Masic, and not Nijaz Mustafic. Both persons exist, so I am saying this just to avoid the confusion. Am I right, sir? Am I right, Mr. Becirovic? You referred to Nijaz Masic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Becirovic, and I am grateful to you, Madam Vidovic, for pointing that out. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, if you could take a look at that document that is before you, Prosecution's Exhibit 79, and that's ERN number 0207-5814. If you could take a look at it and tell the Trial Chamber whether or not you recognise this document. Have you seen it before, before coming to the Tribunal, to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I saw this document for the first time several days ago, upon my arrival in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Becirovic, if you could take a look at number 8, the list of persons. There are a list of persons on this document. Please take a look at number 8. It states Department for Communication, Hamed Alic. Does that accurately reflect what you know about Mr. Alic, that he was, in fact, in the department for communication and he was the head of that department?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that Hamed Alic was ever a member of the communication department. I'm trying to say that I didn't know that at this time, September of 1992, there was any such establishment as this department. As far as I know, Hamed Alic was in charge of the service for communications and information, which as far as I was aware, was -- existed within the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to bring your attention to number 6, the 6th person on the list. Do you know that person, Ramiz Becirovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this name and last name. This is my brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your brother in Srebrenica during the period of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Ramiz arrived in Srebrenica in October, in the second half of October of 1992. And up until then, he was in the Suceska local commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And was he a member of either the War Presidency or the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the Territorial Defence in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise any other names on this list, other than the 6th and 8?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I know most of these people, most of the people from the list. I see the name Nijaz Masic mentioned here, which is the same person who was gathering or collecting statements from the victims in the PTT building. I know other persons as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Who else do you know on the list?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know all of the persons on the list. I know some better, some less. The person listed under 7, I knew the least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you familiar with Dr. -- with Nedret Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met him in 1992 when he arrived from Tuzla in Srebrenica. This is a physician who did a lot to help the ill and the wounded in Srebrenica deal with their injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the ones you have already told us about, the others that you do know that are on the list, were they members of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say either way. I knew some people even before 1992. I got to know some people better after 1993, or after the demilitarisation, therefore, I cannot claim that all of them were members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Next I would like the witness to be shown Prosecution Exhibit 100. And this document is also presently on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could -- Mr. Becirovic, could you take a look at that document, Prosecution's Exhibit 100. It's ERN 0180-1586 to 1587. This document is dated July 2nd, 1992. And could you tell the Trial Chamber whether you have seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number, the ERN number, because the number that you gave us, I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, actually, the ERN probably corresponds to the English, so I will give you the --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. We're trying to sort out the ERN number at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document that you are looking at now, Prosecution Exhibit 100, let's try to determine whether we're both looking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What I suggest, just to make -- to put our minds at rest on this: Usher, could you please put on the ELMO for a few seconds the document in B/C/S that the witness has in front of him. No --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you turn to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- it's not this page for sure. It's not the first one. It's not this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The next page, if you turn again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's not that one. It's not that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Still not the same one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not that one either. Yes, I think it's this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document that was given to us as P100, and it seems not just to us but to all of you, actually consists of a number of documents, each of them containing a P number. I believe this would lead to a lot of confusion later on, therefore I asked the Prosecutor to give us the number of this document, 11/92, dated the 7th of July, 1992. Because this will create problems for all of us. P100 is an entirely different document from the one you are trying to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are one hundred per cent right again and I am grateful to you, Ms. Vidovic. The other problem is that, looking at this particular page, I see two numbers, top right corner. One is 0100159, and it looks likes 6. Then just below -- now I lost it. And below the stamp, always on the top right corner, then there is 02066405. So first of all, I think we need to know what we are talking about, which is -- we need to have the correct number of this document and -- by reference to the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Pardon me. I will do the best I can by way of an explanation. It appears this document may have been ERN stamped twice. So what I propose is that I just read out the ERN number and we may have to give this another -- at this point I am advised we cannot give it another ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has already been given a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me just read out the ERN number, Your Honour. It's 0206-6405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I can be of assistance, our case manager says that this is P270.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I am advised it is also P100. I'm not sure where the confusion is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a case of a dual personality here. Typical of international law. Anyway, we now know and the witness knows precisely which document you are being referred to. So you can actually follow the question that will be put to you by Ms. Richardson. Can you put that page on the desk in front of the witness, please, Madam Usher, and thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this document is also in Sanction, Your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, can you take a look at this document and tell the Trial Chamber whether or not you've scene this document before.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I saw this document a few days ago for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My first question to you, Mr. Becirovic, is whether or not, from looking at the document, could you tell how this document -- whether or not this document was transmitted and how that was done.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose, judging by the telephone number in the left upper corner, that this document may have been faxed through. I'm not claiming that it was since, during this period of time, I was not in a position to -- to be in the room where the fax machine was. And I believe that at that time the telephone lines were still operating and one could use them to talk to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. A matter of clarification. I am now following the English version of the text, and looking at line 9 and 10 of page 23, it seems that the telephone number that the witness refers to, according to the transcript, is in the left upper corner. Now, looking at this document, there is no telephone number on the top left upper corner. There is what seems to me a telephone number, the bottom left corner. I stand to be corrected on this, but I think it needs to be clarified. Is it top left or bottom left?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, on the B/C/S document it is the top left, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but why doesn't it appear --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it appears to be a translation matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I see again the B/C/S version, please. Can you put it on the ELMO for a while, please. All right. That is... Case assistant, can you zoom-in that number, please, for us a little bit. Top. Yes. 886250, yes. Okay. Now can we see the English version, please. It doesn't -- for the record, therefore, we must make it clear that unless it is hidden behind -- this is again already zoomed-in a little bit. Can we see it in its original format? Let me see if it's... You can give it back to the witness. Now I would like to see the English version on the ELMO. I know it is on Sanction, but on Sanction it has already been... Now it's the full page. Now the full page, and the number doesn't appear on the English version. So for the record, that is being stated by the Trial Chamber for all intents and purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should submit at this point that we will do another translation of this document and resubmit it, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. It's important because it -- the witness has mentioned that, in his opinion, this must have been or probably was faxed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, where was the fax machine in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the telephone lines working in July?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the month? Did you say June or July?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: July of 1992. At least the early part of 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure of the date when the telephone lines were finally interrupted. As far as I can remember, it was either late June or early July, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you take a look at this document, the fourth paragraph down, that talks about communication, communication and information. It states that, "At the same meeting the communication and information service was formed which should cover the municipality of Srebrenica and Bratunac. This decision was made because the forces of Bratunac TO did not have any possibilities to inform the public." The next line states: "Hamed Alic was appointed the chief of this service." "The service has the task to ensure communications with BH TO staff and regional staff and ensure the rest of the time with families of the TO combat and other citizens." Is this accurate? When I say "this," I mean with respect to the communication of -- the communication between families that the communication and information service did, in fact, perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm concerned that the line of questioning pursued by my learned friend is going to lead to confusion and if not might even mislead this witness. He has said at least twice that as far as he knows Hamed Alic was performing a service of communication information service which was within the War Presidency. And he has been asked that several times and the last time he was shown a document he said I'm not aware that Hamed Alic was ever a member of the communication department --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was such department actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- and it was within the War Presidency. Now, I don't know if my learned friend is trying to get him to change that answer by showing him a series of documents, but in any event, even if we look at this document, it refers to a War Presidency being formed, it refers to various people having various functions in the War Presidency, and it is certainly not clear -- or at least in our submission it is clear that that communication information service is the one within the War Presidency. Now the problem with the way my learned friend is putting the question is she's simply asking was the communication service -- but we have to be clear at least whether we're talking about the War Presidency communication service or something else. And in any event, this witness has given clear answers on several occasions and seems as if it's a futile exercise to show him document after document and ask him the same question about whether he knows the communication service was established. He's answered there was one, it was within the War Presidency. So I really don't see where this is going and I do fear that it may lead to confusion at this rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let's rephrase the question, Ms. Richardson, putting it in a neutral form, referring to what is described in this document as the communications and information service, irrespective of whether it was in the Territorial Staff or whether it was in the Operation Staff or whether it was in the War Presidency. Assuming that there was such a communication and information service, would you agree, Mr. Becirovic, that these were the terms of reference of that service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The service for communications and information existed and, if I told you what the essence of its work was maybe I could help you resolve this problem. What I would like to say is that the essence of the work of the service in 1992 and 1993 was to send information on the families or family members who had been deported or expelled from the municipality of Bratunac to those who resided in the territory of Tuzla. And also the other two activities that I mentioned a while ago, that was gathering statements from the eye witnesses and recording, by way of an amateur camera, the details depicting the destruction of the town by the Serbian forces at the moment when they were leaving Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you both happy with this, Mr. Jones and Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy with that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm happy with all of the witness's answers to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown another document, Prosecution's Exhibit 117, and that is ERN 01239505 to 01295. I think it is a one-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, have you seen this -- Mr. Becirovic, if you take a look at this document, could you tell the Trial Chamber whether you've seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I saw this document for the first time a few days ago, here in The Hague. I was not familiar with its contents before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you're familiar with Captain Velid Sabic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Velid Sabic for the first time in August 1992, I believe. We didn't talk. We just met passing by each other. After that, he went to Tuzla, and after that I didn't see him until after 1995, and even after then, I only saw him rarely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he prior to coming to Srebrenica, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the area of Konjevic Polje, residing in the village where he was born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what municipality is Konjevic Polje located in?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the western part of Bratunac municipality that was not occupied by the Serbs in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the very last paragraph of this document. Just for the record, the document is dated the 16th of July, 1992. The subject matter is "Decisions by the Bratunac TO Staff." I will just read for you the relevant portion I would like you to consider. "Because objective circumstances are such that the Bratunac TO is unable to keep the public informed, it is agreed --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The Prosecutor interprets the document wrongly. It doesn't say that this was passed by the Bratunac TO. This was a meeting of the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff and the TO Staff are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I believe I -- unless the translation is incorrect, I said "the subject," and I'm reading from the document in English, "Decision by the Bratunac TO Staff." So unless there is a -- there is some kind of misunderstanding by the Defence I'm not sure what the Defence is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I have in the transcript here, at line 21, 22, the subject is -- reporting what you said, "The subject matter is 'Decisions by the Bratunac TO Staff.'" Now, the text -- the English version of the document that I am seeing, that I have, at the top, as a title -- not as a title. At the top it has "Republic of Bosnia-Hercegovina, Bratunac Municipality Territorial Defence Staff, number 5/92." If that is wrong in translation of what there is in the Serbo-Croat version, please point that out. I don't have the Serbo-Croat version in front of me. Perhaps you could put it on the ELMO a little bit, Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Maybe it would be best for the witness to look at the text, the first paragraph, where it says: "At the meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Bratunac TO, which was held on the 16th of July, 1992/3, decisions were adopted." Maybe it would be best for the witness to look at the document, because in this case, as well as in the other cases, the Prosecutor is trying to pull out sentences from the context of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the meaning of "Predmet"? THE WITNESS? [Interpretation] "Subject."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it seems to me, looking at the document, looking at the document, that at the top it says: Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- I can't read it -- "Opstinski Stab." It's -- "stab" is "staff" definitely. "TO Bratunac." So I don't know how to translate that because it is not my responsibility in any case. Then the subject is definitely the "Odluke Staba Bratunac." So the subject matter -- perhaps someone can translate. What does the title -- how would the title read out in English?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Subject: Decisions of the staff of the Territorial Defence of Bratunac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And the top part is Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And what is the second line, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of Bratunac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So now we can put the English version again on Sanction, please. Yes. I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the essence of my objection was the following: The Prosecution is saying that at the meeting of the staff of the TO Bratunac, the decisions were passed. However, it transpires from the first part of the text that these decisions were adopted at the meeting of the Crisis Staff. And this is the essence of my objection. It is summed up with the first sentence, which has been interpreted wrongly by the Prosecutor and the Prosecutor then used his -- her wrong interpretation to put her question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. There is no doubt that the first line of the substantive part of the document does say three decisions were adopted at a meeting of the Bratunac TO Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't dispute that that is what it says. I simply am using a document, going to the relevant portions so we will be here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go straight to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm making it clear that supposedly the decisions that were taken here were taken according to the document by the -- at a meeting of the Bratunac TO Crisis Staff. Let's proceed. Could you repeat your question now because we have lost track of it and you hadn't even started asking the question, as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I believe when I -- prior to the objection I -- could I have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You hadn't started the...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could take a look at the last paragraph. That's the portion of the document that I will ask you a question about. Now, this document states that communication, there were communication problems -- well, let me just read it, again, so that there is no misunderstanding. I'm reading from the English version: "Because objective circumstances are such that the Bratunac TO is unable to keep the public informed, it was agreed previously that all tasks involving communications and information will be taken over by the service in Srebrenica." It goes on to state: "Hamed Alic was appointed chief of the service for communication and information." Mr. Becirovic, my question to you is: During this period of time, I believe you testified that a number of people -- that a number of Muslims had been deported from Bratunac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so does this paragraph reflect -- well, and as a result of that deportation, that it was difficult -- communication was difficult in that area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We spent an hour yesterday on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any other questions with respect to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He explained how they moved from gathering intelligence on to something completely different, which is precisely what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can move to another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Prosecution's Exhibit 9, if that could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. At this time, Mr. Becirovic, I would like you to take a look at the document before you, Prosecution's Exhibit 9, ERN number 01239519 - 0123-9520 and ask you if you have seen this document before and are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I saw this document a few days ago here in The Hague, for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. With respect to this document, which is -- I would just like to read the date, which is dated 15th of October, 1992, Republic -- top left-hand corner, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebrenica armed forces staff. It also says "strictly confidential." I would like to draw your attention to the third portion, what is numbered number 3, the third section of this document, which states: "The following independent units of the combat and support arms shall be formed." C of that subsection states "communication platoon." My question to you is whether or not you were aware that a communication platoon had been formed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One thing: I would prefer if my learned friend would say are you aware of whether a platoon was formed. We don't presuppose that anything that is purportedly occurring in this document actually occurred. In other words, that can't be accepted as a fact that it was -- that it was established and the only question is whether this witness knows about it, is he aware whether that happened at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be a more proper question. Again, it doesn't change much, but at the end of the day it is a proper question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I can rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, do you know if a communication platoon was formed in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this period of time, which is referred to within this document, it wasn't, as far as I know. There was no communications platoon. Some units were formed after the demilitarisation in 1994, 1995. Up to then, there were only groups of people that people referred to as people from Potocari, Naser's men, people from Suceska or men from Suceska. And if I may note that if, in this period, if there had been so many units, platoons and brigades, the genocide that happened in 1995 would never have happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the communications, the individuals who worked in communication, at around this time period, how many were there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any other group of people who would be performing the communications tasks, save for my group, the group that I was a member of during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions, Your Honour, with respect to this document. Thank you, Mr. Becirovic. All right. Thank you. I would like to move to another subject matter. Again, though, keeping in mind Mr. Hamed Alic as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What instructions did you receive from Mr. Hamed Alic during 1992, if any?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive any instructions from Mr. Hamed Alic. At that time I had in mind what he had been through in 1992 and because of the fact that he slept in the PTT, that I could tell him what I was doing. Most of his friends and family were deported to Tuzla. His daughter was in Zivinice. So all that I did, Hamed Alic knew what it was and he never asked me to do anything else other than what I was doing anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he -- did, at any point in time, did he himself come to you to send any messages?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in late July, 1992, after the telephone lines were broken down, and afterwards a bit more often, the information was drafted mostly for the public, for the media and television of Bosnia-Herzegovina, stating that the state organs are to be informed of the events. And in the previously described manner in which I communicated with the ham operators, these messages were sent. So I would read the text into the microphone and the operator in Sarajevo would either write it down or tape it, and then this information was then transmitted through Murat Efendic who was a member of the War Presidency of Srebrenica but lived in Sarajevo. This information was delivered to the Presidency and state organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as radio and television of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hamed Alic brought you messages to communicate to Mr. Efendic in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is while you were being supervised by him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. While he was in Srebrenica. And I think that in December of 1992 he left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did he bring messages to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, initially that was seldom. Perhaps one or two messages a week. However, that actually depended on the situation and to what extent the Serbs attacked and how aggressively. If we had a very intense infantry or artillery attack and if we had a lot of wounded and injured, then information would be sent on a daily basis. I would like to especially highlight January, February and March of 1993 when there was hunger in Srebrenica, when people were dying of hunger. At that time we tried to send a message about what was going on in Srebrenica, about people dying there. We wanted this information to reach the world so that the world could help us. In that period of time, we sent messages perhaps even more often, once or twice a day, depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "that period of time," could you -- well, could you just give us the range of months in 1992 that he gave you messages. Was it from July until he left in December, or after that? Or in August?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've mentioned that this was from late July, then throughout August, September, October, and November, and I think that he left Srebrenica in December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he get this -- these messages? From where did he get the information that he brought to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether somebody brought the information to him or whether he wrote it himself. At the time, I didn't think it necessary for me to know the origin of the information. I felt it my duty to transmit the information to the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just on one matter. The interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In English, at lines 3 to 4, the witness said -- he referred to what extent the Serbs attacked and how aggressively, and he said, "If we had a very intense infantry or artillery attack..." I understand in Bosnian it's clear that that means obviously if we received, if we were the subjects of an attack, that this is referring to attacks by Serbs exclusively. From the English it may be ambiguous, but that is certainly our understanding from the Bosnian, and it probably is clear from the context since it is referring to Serb attacks, but just lest there be any doubt, we're referring to Serb attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, actually, but thank you for your remark, but I don't think we need to do anything about it. Thanks. Let's proceed, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the subject matter of these messages that you received from Mr. Hamed Alic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, the subject matter was the very difficult epidemiological situation: Hunger, lack of proper sanitary facilities, various illnesses that were rampant at the time. That was the essence of the information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else bring you -- well, I just have one more question with respect to Mr. Hamed Alic. Did he bring you -- the messages, were they written down or were they oral messages that he gave you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He brought messages written down, on a paper. He did not relate them to me verbally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you only send messages from him to Sarajevo or did you send messages from him to other places?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The Prosecutor ought to ask or specify the period of time, because it is obvious, based on the testimony of this witness, that the situation changed from one period to another. Therefore, the Prosecutor ought to specify the time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I think there is -- I think the witness needs to answer my first question and then we can -- I think I had asked him whether or not... I see what the point that the Defence is making, so I can ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. I think it is fair enough, so we need to establish that. In any case it can be established either way, I think. Because the witness can answer your question and then you can proceed with asking him, Could you specify or put these in a time frame. Perhaps now that he has heard the exchange, he can answer the question by referring to specific time periods or time frames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand the question, Mr. Becirovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go ahead. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Initially, perhaps up until December of 1992, the information mostly went to Sarajevo. Less often to other destinations. However, after December of 1992, to a smaller extent, the information would also be sent to Tuzla for the media, for the radio and television of the Tuzla canton, and also to the ham operators. In December and then in January, February and March of 1993 I established contact with ham radio operators in Zagreb, where journalists from some Western newspapers would assemble occasionally and gather information. And sometimes, when the situation was rather critical in certain other battlefields in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there would be perhaps a group of CNN journalists sitting in Sarajevo and requesting information about what was going on in Srebrenica. I think it is important to state here that in February of 1993, I believe, a photo journalist from Germany, Phillip von Recklinghausen, came to Srebrenica from Tuzla and with his camera he recorded many important things, in my view, and this was a testament to what was going on. In addition to him, there was also a BBC crew with Tony Birtley there. Tony Birtley I think spent in Srebrenica more than a month. He was wounded there by shrapnel off a shell fired by the Serbs. He was evacuated together with another military observer, UN military observer, who had been wounded. I believe that the observer's name was McDonald. There they we're evacuated via Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have a question of clarification. I think you have been asked whether you transmitted certain messages which have been given to you from Hamed Alic to other places than Sarajevo. Now you told us about what has been transmitted in January, February, March, but a couple of minutes ago you had told us that Hamed Alic had left, according to your knowledge, Srebrenica in December. Now, did he still, even from the outside, give you messages to be sent somewhere or when you had to send messages after December, they have been given to you to be transmitted by other persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for giving a lengthy answer to things that may perhaps be asked only later. While Hamed Alic was in Srebrenica, as I've mentioned, the information I received from him I mostly sent to Sarajevo. In November of 1992, or perhaps several weeks before Hamed Alic left Srebrenica, there were also some messages that went to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start sending messages to Mr. Efendic in Sarajevo? Do you remember the time? The month?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was in August of 1992. I can't remember precisely. Perhaps a bit earlier, perhaps a bit later, but if it was earlier, then not much earlier. Perhaps in late July or early August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you relayed messages to Mr. Efendic, did you relay them to him directly or did you first relay them to an operator who then relayed them to Mr. Efendic? Could you just tell us how this worked.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several locations in Sarajevo where Murat could receive information. Therefore, there were several radio clubs. He mostly sat next to the radio ham operators receiving information. I think that in a radio club called 4 SGS, there was an operator --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and in that location Murat was not needed because the two of them knew each other really well and this operator could keep the information and give it to Murat once he saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. Just before I resume my questioning, I understand that the Prosecution will be translating the -- Prosecution's Exhibit 100, so that we will provide a translation to that entire exhibit, Your Honour, at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, prior to the break, you were testifying about the communications that you had with Mr. Efendic in 1992. Did you also have communications with him in 1993 as well? When I say "communication," by that I mean, were you also sending him messages?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I continued communicating or sending messages to Murat Efendic in 1993 and 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you send messages as well to Tuzla? Messages -- and let me be clear, messages from Mr. Hamed Alic or messages that you yourself sent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because let's clarify this first. In answering the previous question, namely in stating that you continued communicating or sending messages to Murat Efendic in 1993, 1994, 1995, on whose behalf were you sending these messages? On your own behalf or on behalf of someone else? Certainly it can't be this Hamed Alic now, because Hamed Alic is, according to you, left more or less on December or just after December 1992. So these continued messages to Efendic, who -- on whose behalf were they in 1993, 1994, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the messages I sent were sent on behalf of the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality. Most of these documents were signed by the service for communications and information, which was under the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So your next question then, which is a repetition of a previous question, actually. I mean, I don't think it needs to be put, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually now that I have -- memory serves me, I think he may have already answered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned or you testified that Mr. Hamed Alic left in December. Could you tell us what happened after he left. Was anyone else assigned to his position as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody else was appointed to his position. Immediately upon his departure, for a week or two we had a vacuum, a gap in sending messages. Although Hamed Alic, on his departure, said that I could write those messages instead of him. However, later on, in agreement with the precedent of the War Presidency, I continued writing messages and sending them on behalf of the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you have this agreement or discussion with the War Presidency about your taking over -- or your continuing to send messages, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an official meeting where somebody or I myself were supposed to be appointed to that position. It's just that at one point in time, president of the War Presidency came into the room where I was and told me that I could write messages which would then be transmitted to the public. And I did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any messages from the War Presidency to transmit in 1992 or in 1993? Please tell us the date.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, if I remember well, already November and December of 1992 and then onwards in 1993, president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic himself wrote certain messages. Those were appeals for humanitarian assistance, appeals for medical aid, or any other type of aid. The places which these messages were supposed to be sent to were the government and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Frequently, Mr. Avdic insisted with Murat Efendic to have this information transmitted also to the UNHCR office in Sarajevo, to UNPROFOR, and sometimes, when the situation was truly dramatic, he urged this information to be transmitted to the Security Council of the UN as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any messages to be sent from anyone from the military?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Never. I never received any messages from the military to transmit it elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive messages from -- did you report on any particular areas, and by that I mean, did you report messages relating to specific areas in Srebrenica and the surrounding villages or even in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have mentioned just now that the subject of the messages, the essence of the messages was to inform the local and international public about the events in Srebrenica, highlighting a very grave humanitarian epidemiological and any other type of circumstances, because we had a lot of people who had been killed, a lot of wounded, a lot of people who were ill with serious illnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you -- did you receive any messages from any particular areas? When I say "areas," I mean in the surrounding Srebrenica and Bratunac areas, from any commanders or anyone in the military forces who were operating in that area?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never received messages from any commanders. At the time, I didn't even think that there were persons who could be referred to as commanders. In my view, those were still poorly organised groups. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I arrived at the information in the following way: Since the post office building was near the hospital where the wounded arrived, as soon as I saw that something was going on, I would go to the hospital, talk to the wounded or to the people who had brought the wounded in, and this is how I acquired information about what was going on, things that I couldn't see myself or hear myself. Any intense shelling launched by Serbs in the area surrounding Srebrenica could also be heard in Srebrenica. Not a day would pass without dozens of shells falling in Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned previously in your testimony that there came a time that Velid Sabic came to Srebrenica. Did you receive any messages from him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that that day when Velid Sabic was in Srebrenica the Serb forces carried out a very intense artillery and later on air attack in the area of Konjevic Polje. In Srebrenica, we could hear the planes flying above and Velid Sabic drafted a very brief note, brought it to me and asked me to transmit it to the media. I did that and this is how I met Velid Sabic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- did you send messages in connection with any military actions undertaken by the Muslim forces or by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
